title: A small langar at home
hookLine: invite someone and feed them, with no agenda

lines: FED FOR NO REASON AT ALL.
cards: Dinner invitations often come with something attached. We should really catch up. I want you to meet my brother.
Let's talk about that project. Nothing wrong with that. But there's another kind: being fed for no reason at all.

No favor to ask, no news to share. Someone just noticed you might be hungry, or tired, or alone, and put a plate in front of you. That kind of meal tends to be remembered, and it's the last langar lesson.
For five days you've been inside the gurdwara's kitchen and its rows. Today it moves into yours.

teach.b: Langar didn't begin as an institution. It began in a household. At Kartarpur, on day forty-one, Guru Nanak farmed his own fields and shared food with whoever came.

teach.h: THE ROW, THE DOOR, THE PLATE.
teach.b: Mata Khivi's kitchen at Khadur was a family kitchen with an open door. Today's huge langars grew out of homes that fed people. So a small langar at home isn't a copy of the real thing.
It's closer to where the real thing started. What makes a meal a langar, even with only two people? This week has the answer.
The pangat: nobody sits higher, so serve your guest the way you'd serve yourself, or better. The open door: the guest doesn't have to earn it or explain it.
A meal everyone can eat: think about what they can eat before what you'd like to cook. Cupped hands: when they try to thank you too much, receive the thanks and let it go. Most of all, no agenda.
You're not recruiting them, fixing them, or networking with them. You're feeding them.
Remember the second pillar from day thirteen, vand chakna, sharing what you have? This is that pillar at your own table. It doesn't have to be fancy.
Dal and rice. A sandwich for a coworker who skipped lunch. Soup for the neighbor home from the hospital.
Look back and the week makes a path: kirtan filled the home, then the row, the open door, the bread, the simple meal, the cupped hands. Now the home fills up again, with a guest.

how: Many Sikh families treat hospitality as an extension of langar, feeding guests and neighbors freely at home, alongside serving in the gurdwara kitchen.

o: sharing what you have with others
keeping your kitchen spotless and tidy
eating only food you cooked yourself

games.q: what's inside the home langar — tap the pairs.
p: Nanak shared food with whoever came

s: langar began as a large institution
it began in households: Guru Nanak at Kartarpur, Mata Khivi at Khadur.
a home langar needs to be a grand meal
dal and rice, a sandwich or a pot of soup will do.
the heart of a home langar is feeding someone with no agenda
not recruiting, fixing or networking. just feeding them.

games.q: you invite a new neighbor for dinner. halfway through, you're tempted to ask them a favor. what makes it a small langar?
o: ask, since they've eaten your food.
leave the favor for another day and just feed them.
hint at it, so they can offer.
games.why: a small langar has no agenda. the meal is the whole point.

practice: Think of one person you could feed: someone who'd be surprised, who's been having a hard time, who's new around here, or who eats alone more than they'd like.
Picture them at your table, on your step, or at their door with a container of food, what you'd make that they could eat and when you'd ask, and hold the picture until it feels possible.
If you pray, you can hold them in your prayers.

wordCard.voice: Vand chakna. Sharing what you have: today, feeding one person, freely, with no agenda. Your week: kirtan at home, pangat, the open door, rotis, a meal everyone can eat, cupped hands, and your own langar.

orig.note: Punjabi, in Gurmukhi script: to share what you have, the second pillar.

carryVoice: Your line: a small langar. Nothing attached, just a plate. Tomorrow, simran on the breath.

sources.ref: Sikh tradition on Guru Nanak at Kartarpur and Mata Khivi at Khadur
Sikh teaching of the three pillars: kirat karni, vand chakna, naam japna
